hints.text: For each point, consider the clockwise semicircle beginning at that point.
Exactly one point can serve as the first endpoint of a containing semicircle, except on probability-zero boundary cases.

solution.setup: Anchor a clockwise semicircle at each sampled point.
solution.reasoning: For a fixed anchor, each of the other four points lands in its clockwise semicircle with probability 1/2, giving 1/16. The five possible anchor events are disjoint almost surely, so multiply by 5.
solution.sanityCheck: The general answer n/2^(n−1) gives 1 for n=2 and decreases as more points are added.

keyInsight: Choose the unique extreme anchor, then use independence for the remaining points.
recognitionCues: Random circular points and containment in a half-circle suggest anchoring at an endpoint.
commonMistakes: Multiplying by five without explaining why the anchor events do not overlap.
followUps: What is the probability the convex hull of three random points contains the center?

source.notes: Original variant of a publicly reported interview family associated with Hudson River Trading, SIG.

title: Five Points in a Semicircle
problem: Five points are chosen independently and uniformly on a circle. What is the probability that all five lie within some semicircle?
